name: Distributed Tracing
intent: Follow one request through every service it touches, as a tree of timed steps, so you can see where the time went and which call failed.
scenario: Checkout takes 3 seconds for some users. One click calls the gateway, the order service, the payment service, the inventory service and two databases. Each team's dashboard looks fine, so nobody knows which hop is slow.
problem: In a system of many services, a single user action becomes dozens of calls. Metrics show that something is slow but not which request or which hop, and logs from different services are separate files. Without a view of the whole path, debugging is guesswork and blame.

howItWorks.title: A trace is a tree of spans
howItWorks.text: A span is one timed operation: an incoming request, an outgoing call, a database query. Each span records its name, start time, duration, status and key attributes. Spans are linked by parent id into a tree, and all spans of one request share a trace id.

howItWorks.title: Pass the trace context on every call
howItWorks.text: When service A calls service B, it sends the trace id and its own span id in a header (the W3C traceparent header is the standard). B starts its span as a child of A's span. If any service forgets to pass the header, the trace is broken at that point.

howItWorks.title: Instrument once with a standard SDK
howItWorks.text: OpenTelemetry provides libraries and automatic instrumentation for common frameworks and clients, so incoming requests, HTTP calls and queries produce spans without custom code. You add manual spans around important work and attributes such as order id or cache hit.

howItWorks.title: Collect, then sample
howItWorks.text: Spans are sent to a collector and stored in a tracing backend (Jaeger, Tempo, a cloud service). Recording every trace for a busy system is expensive, so you sample: keep a small percentage of normal traces, and keep all slow or failed ones (tail-based sampling).

howItWorks.title: Read the waterfall
howItWorks.text: A trace view shows spans as bars on a timeline. A long bar is slow work; a gap between a parent and its children is time spent in the parent itself; children laid out one after another show calls that could run in parallel. The critical path is the chain of spans that determines the total time.

pros: Shows exactly where time is spent across services
Makes failures and retries visible in context
Reveals hidden sequential calls and unexpected dependencies
Links to logs through the trace id
cons: Every service and every client library must propagate the context
Instrumentation adds some overhead, and storage is costly without sampling
Sampling can drop the very trace you wanted unless you keep slow and error traces
Traces across queues and batch jobs need extra care to stay connected
whenToUse: Systems with several services, where one request crosses many of them
Investigating latency, errors and retries that no single service owns
Understanding dependencies and the critical path of a user action
whenNotToUse: A single process or a small monolith, where profiling and logs may be enough
As a substitute for metrics when you need rates and trends over weeks
pitfalls: A service that drops the trace header, which splits one trace into unrelated pieces
Sampling by a fixed percentage so rare errors are rarely kept
Putting personal data or secrets into span attributes
Having traces but no link from log lines to the trace id

roles.label: Service
roles.description: Creates spans and passes the trace context on.

roles.label: Trace store
roles.description: Stores traces and draws the waterfall.

quiz.question: A search request takes 900 ms. Its trace shows the gateway span covering the whole time. Under it, three child spans for the ranker, the profile service and the ads service run strictly one after another, about 270 ms each, and none of them uses the output of another. What is the most useful conclusion?
options: The ranker is the bottleneck and should get more instances, since it is the first and therefore most important child span.
The three calls are independent, so issuing them in parallel could cut the time to about the slowest one.
The gateway adds most of the delay itself, because its span is the longest bar in the trace.
The trace is incomplete, because healthy children would overlap each other on the timeline.
quiz.explanation: Children laid out end to end that do not depend on each other are a sign of avoidable sequential calls, so the critical path can shrink to roughly 270 ms. The gateway bar is long only because it contains its children, so it is not the cause.

quiz.question: A payments platform handles 2 million requests a day and keeps 1 percent of traces, chosen at random when each request starts. About 0.05 percent of requests fail with a rare timeout, and engineers can almost never find an example trace of one. What change fixes this best?
options: Raise the random rate from 1 percent to 10 percent so that ten times more of the rare failures are caught.
Move spans into application logs, which are always kept in full and can be searched by request id.
Replace traces with a latency metric, since a counter records every failing request.
Use tail-based sampling at the collector so every slow or failed trace is kept.
quiz.explanation: Tail-based sampling decides after the trace finishes, so it can keep all the errors and slow requests cheaply. A higher random rate still keeps only a tenth of the rare failures and costs ten times the storage.

quiz.question: Checkout calls the gateway, the order service and the payment service, and one trace shows all three. The order service then puts a message on a queue, and the worker that consumes it appears in the backend as a separate, unrelated trace with a new trace id. What is the right fix?
options: Copy the trace context into the message headers when publishing, and extract it in the consumer before it starts its span.
Give the worker a bigger collector buffer so its spans can be matched to the original trace later.
Log the order id in the worker and join the two traces by hand when someone investigates.
Raise the sampling rate on the worker so its spans are more likely to be stored.
quiz.explanation: Trace context travels in a header, and a queue message needs the same treatment: inject on publish, extract on consume. Without it, the worker starts a new trace. Manual joining by order id works once but gives no waterfall.
